reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Wyatt stood at the bus stop with Grandma. The sun was out. It was sunny. "My shadow is big," said Wyatt. He zipped his jacket up, up, up.

Then the wind came. It blew his hat right off. "Come back, hat!" laughed Wyatt. Grandma caught it. "It is windy," she said. The wind made the leaves spin and spin.

Dark clouds rolled in. Rain began to fall. Plop, plop on Wyatt's boots. Then he heard a big rumble. Thunder! Grandma said, "When you hear thunder, go indoors." Wyatt grabbed her hand. "Indoors, indoors!" They ran to the cafe next to the bus stop. They watched the rain from the warm window. "Good thinking," said Grandma. Wyatt munched his snack and smiled. "I listened to the thunder."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Sarah was at Grandma's house. Ten red apples sat in a basket. Grandma had a big jar of cookies. "You may have cookies today," said Grandma. "But first, let's count the apples. Then we will count the cookies too."

Sarah pointed at the apples. She counted from the left side. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Grandma smiled. Then Sarah's cat jumped up. The cat knocked one apple out. Now there were nine apples and a dirty apple on the floor. Grandma poured water into a bowl and washed it. "Try counting from the other side," said Grandma.

Sarah pointed at the right side now. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine." Nine again. Sarah clapped her hands. "Same number, Grandma!" Then they counted the cookies. There were five cookies and nine apples. "The apples have more," said Sarah. Grandma gave her two cookies and kept the rest. Sarah shared one cookie with Grandma. "We have the same now," said Sarah. Grandma took a big, happy bite.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Brielle got to school early. She sat down at the little table. Time to write her name!

Miss Ana gave her a fat pencil. "Hold it like this," said Miss Ana. She showed Brielle how to pinch the pencil near the top.

Brielle tried. The pencil wiggled. The B looked like a squiggle. She tried again. This time the B stood up tall.

Then Brielle stood up to get more paper. She waved the pencil as she walked. "Whoa," said Miss Ana. "Point it down. Carry a pencil with the point facing down so it cannot poke anyone."

Brielle looked at the pencil. She turned the point down. She walked carefully past her friend Milo. No poke! "That was almost a joke," said Milo, and he laughed.

Brielle sat back down. She wrote B, then R, then I. "Count the letters with me," she said. "One, two, three." She kept writing. BRIELLE!

"I did it," said Brielle, holding up her paper.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Charlotte went to the library with her dad. On a big table there were three signs. One said "Animals." One said "Toys." One said "Foods."

Charlotte picked up a toy car and put it under "Toys." Then she found a soft bear and put it under "Animals." "What goes under Foods?" she wondered.

She found a basket of picture cards. There was an apple card. There was a bread card. And there was a carrot card. Charlotte put the carrot under "Toys." It looked silly next to the teddy bear!

A boy named Sam ran over. "Hey!" he did not yell. "Carrots are foods," he said. "Like apples and bread." Charlotte looked at the carrot. Then she looked at the apple. Then the bread.

She picked up the carrot and moved it. She put it under "Foods" with the apple and the bread. Sam clapped. Charlotte spun the wheel on the toy car. Round and round it went.

"Can we eat a book?" Charlotte asked her dad. Dad laughed. "No, books are not foods." Charlotte held the apple card up high. "This one is!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Mila sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her curly hair bounced as she looked around. She saw a poster of a dog on the wall. She saw a jar of stickers by the sink.

"Today you get a shot," said Mom.

Mila shook her head. She thought a shot would be big. She thought it would hurt for a long time. She hid her arm behind her back.

The nurse came in with a small tray. On the tray was a very thin needle. It was small like a tiny straw. Mila looked at it. It did not look big at all.

"It is a quick poke in the arm," said the nurse. "Then it is done."

Mila held Mom's hand. She pulled up her sleeve. The nurse touched her arm. Mila felt one small poke, quick as that.

"All done!" said the nurse.

Mila looked at her arm. There was a tiny round bandage on it. She had waited for something big. But it was just one quick poke.

The nurse did not hurry away. She sat down and smiled. "You can pick a sticker now," she said.

Mila picked a sticker of a yellow dog. She put it on her sleeve, right over the bandage. Then she waved her arm in the air.

"My arm is quick and brave," said Mila.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Lennon went to the store with Mama. Yesterday, Lennon had a cough. Today, her cough was just a tiny squeak, like a weak little mouse. So today they could go out.

Lennon saw a stuffed mouse on the shelf. It was gray and soft. "I want to hold it now," she said. Mama picked it up and turned it over. "This is for Mia," said Mama. "It is her birthday present. We give it to her tomorrow." Lennon hugged the mouse. She did not want to put it down. "Not now?" she whispered. "Not now," said Mama. "First we sleep. Then it will be tomorrow."

They bought the mouse and put it in the bag. At home, Lennon ate soup. Then she slept and slept. When she woke up, the sun was in a new place in the sky. "Is it tomorrow?" she asked. Mama smiled and lifted her up. "Yes. Today is the day after yesterday. Come on, let's go." Lennon carried the bag to Mia's house all by herself. Mia opened the door. Lennon held out the mouse. "Happy birthday, Mia," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Ayla sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted to feel brave, but she felt a little mad about the wait. A balloon floated near the ceiling. She saw it with her eyes. "Look, Mommy," she said. A baby cried, and Ayla heard it with her ears. The room smelled like soap. She noticed that with her nose. The doctor looked in Ayla's mouth. "Say ahh," she said. Ayla tasted the wooden stick, just a little. Then the doctor held Ayla's hand. "Squeeze my fingers," she said. Ayla felt the squeeze with her fingers. Then the doctor said, "Shoes off, please. Let me see your toes." Ayla took off her shoes and socks.

After the visit, Mommy walked Ayla home. In the backyard, Ayla took off her shoes again. She stepped on the grass. "It tickles, Mommy!" she said. "My feet feel it too!" Mommy laughed and took off her own shoes. They stood in the soft grass together. "Wiggle your toes," said Mommy. Ayla wiggled them. The grass tickled and tickled.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Mateo ran into Grandma's house. "Where is the baby?" he asked. Grandma pointed to the soft chair. Papa sat there, holding a tiny bundle. It was the new baby. It was Mateo's baby sister.

"I want to hold her!" said Mateo. He reached up on his tippy toes. The baby was too far away. He jumped. Still too far. "You can hold her," said Papa, "but you have to sit down on the couch. And I will sit right beside you and help."

Mateo sat on the couch. Papa sat next to him. Papa placed the baby in Mateo's arms. "Hello, baby," Mateo whispered. The baby made a little mouth, like a fish. Mateo laughed. Her hand popped out of the blanket and tickled his chin, so small and warm.

"She is squeezing my finger!" Mateo said. Grandma brought a glass of water for Papa. "Big brother, you are doing a good job," she said. The baby yawned a great big yawn. Her eyes closed. Mateo held still, very still, like a stone. Papa smiled and whispered, "She likes your arms." Mateo grinned and looked down at his sleeping sister. "Stay right there," he told her softly.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Leah stood in the pool changing room. She was putting on her swimsuit. Today she would learn to swim. "I hope I can do it," she said. Mom held her hand. They walked out to the pool. The water was big and blue.

Leah saw a tall chair by the water. A man sat up in it. "Why does he sit so high?" Leah asked Mom. "Look and see," said Mom. Leah watched. From up high, the man could see every swimmer. Then a boy splashed too far out. The man blew his whistle. He climbed down fast. He helped the boy back to the wall. "He saw him from up there!" said Leah. She waved at the man. He waved back.

Leah got in the water. She kicked her legs. She blew bubbles. She was quiet and careful. The man in the tall chair watched her too. "I did it!" Leah called. Then, splash, a drop of water went right in her eye. The man saw it happen. He was already walking over. "Here is a towel," he said. Leah smiled. He really did watch everyone.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Hudson stood in the big school gym. A red hoop lay on the floor. He had a blue beanbag in his hand. He wanted it to land in the hoop.

Hudson threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew past the hoop. It landed far away with a soft sound. "Oh no," said Hudson. "How will I get it in?"

His teacher, Miss Kim, came over. She picked up her own beanbag. "Watch me," she said. "This is an underhand toss." Her arm swung from low down. It swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed into the hoop. Hudson's mouth opened wide.

"I want to try that!" he said. He held his beanbag low. His arm swung from low down, forward and up. The beanbag went up and over. Plip. It landed in the hoop. "I did it!" said Hudson. Miss Kim clapped.

Then she rolled him a big yellow ball. Hudson held out both hands. The ball bounced off his chest. He ran after it. "Messy try!" he laughed. He tried again with both hands open wide. This time the ball landed right in them. Hudson hugged the ball tight.

"Again, please!" he said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Asher ran to the big red slide. He was so excited. "My turn, my turn!" he said. He climbed up the steps. Then a big boy pushed past him. Asher fell down on his bottom. His face felt hot. His hands made tight fists. He was angry.

Asher stomped off the slide. He wanted to yell. His grandma sat on the bench. "Come here, Asher," she said. "Let's try slow, big breaths." Asher sat next to her. Grandma took a slow breath in. Asher copied her. He blew the air out, slow and long. They did it again. In and out, like a big balloon.

Asher unclenched his fists. His body felt calm now. "I feel better," he said. He looked back at the slide. The big boy had gone to the swings. "You can go up now," said Grandma.

Asher climbed the steps again. He saw the whole playground from the top. He slid down fast and laughed. "I did it!" he said. Grandma clapped her hands in a big circle. "Hooray for Asher!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Adam wanted a story about a storm. He ran to his room with his big book. "Daddy, read this one!"

Daddy sat on the bed. Adam snuggled close. The lamp made a warm, soft circle of light.

Adam pointed at the page. "What does it say?" He put his finger on the right side of the page. He slid his finger to the left.

Daddy smiled. He took Adam's hand. "Start here," he said. He set Adam's finger on the left side. Then he moved it along, slow and smooth. "The words go this way."

Adam tried it himself. Left to right, just like Daddy. Then Daddy read the words out loud. The words said "A big storm is coming." Adam gasped. The marks on the page had told Daddy what to say!

"It knows the storm story," said Adam. "The little marks talk to you?"

"Yes," said Daddy. "They talk to whoever reads them."

Adam turned one page. Then another page. The story went on and on. He found the stinky skunk at the end, after the storm. Then they came to the last page.

"The end," said Daddy. He closed the book.

Adam yawned. "Don't forget the storm book tomorrow," he said. He hugged it tight to his chest.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Ethan ran up to the bookmobile. The door was open wide. He wanted his very own library card.

Inside, the shelves were tall, tall, tall. The books were big and thick. Ethan could not reach them at all. He stood on his tiptoes. His fingers touched only air.

Then he saw something. A little corner with a tiny rug. The rug was squishy under his feet. Small shelves stood there, just his size. Every book had big, bright pictures.

"This is the children's area," said the driver. "The books here are just for young kids like you."

Ethan grabbed a book about trucks. He hugged it tight. The driver gave him a shiny new card.

"Can I take the truck book home?" Ethan asked.

"You sure can," said the driver. She put the book in a bag. The bag covered it up like a blanket.

Ethan held the bag all the way home. "Truck book, meet my lunch," he said. He set them side by side on the table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Maya ran to the park with her teddy bear, Ben. She saw her friend Leo by the big tree. Leo had a stick in his hand.

"I am flying a plane," said Leo. He held up his flat piece of bark. It was not a plane at all. Maya looked hard. Then Leo ran in a circle. "Zoom, zoom!" he said. The bark went up and down in his hand.

Maya laughed. "I know what to do," she said. She put Ben on a flat rock. The rock was her house now. She made a bed with leaves. "Shh, Ben is sleeping," she said. Leo tapped the rock with his stick. Maya said, "Knock, knock! Who is it?" Leo said, "It is the pilot!" Maya clapped.

Then a real wind came. It blew the leaves off Ben's bed. Maya gasped. "My house is losing its roof!" Leo held his bark over Ben. "Now it is a roof," he said. The wind stopped. The leaves lay flat on the grass.

"I love this game," said Maya. "The bark is a plane. The rock is a house. None of it is real. But we play like it is!" Leo smiled and flew his plane round and round. Maya hugged Ben tight. "Time for dinner, Ben," she said. "Knock, knock on our rock house."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Isaiah sat in the school library with his teacher, Ms. Rao. He wanted to find his own name in a book. But he could not read the letters yet.

"Let's start with the first letter," said Ms. Rao. "I. It says i, like in igloo." Isaiah looked at the big black letters on the page. Then he found a card with his name. But the first letter was small. "That is not right," said Isaiah. Ms. Rao smiled. "Your name starts with a capital I," she said. She took out a red crayon. Isaiah drew a big capital I over the small one. Now it said Isaiah, just right.

He held the card up high. The lamp made the letters shine. "I did it," said Isaiah. Ms. Rao clapped. "Now let's find the S," she said. Isaiah turned the page. "S says sss," he said, like a snake. "Yes," said Ms. Rao. Isaiah laughed and pointed at the next letter. "That one is A!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Bennett was going to be a big brother. Grandma was knitting a small blue sock. Grandpa was painting a small white crib. Bennett wanted to help too.

"Can I pick a gift for the baby?" he asked. "Yes," said Grandma. "Let's go to the baby store." At the store, Bennett saw soft blankets. He saw tiny hats. Then he saw a big stack of diapers, tall as a tower.

A boy next to him pointed at the tower. "Why so many diapers?" he asked his mom. "Babies wear diapers because they cannot use the toilet yet," she said. Bennett listened. He looked at the tower again. So babies need diapers, he thought. One after another after another.

Bennett picked out a pack of diapers. He picked a little pencil and a pad of paper too. At home, he asked Grandpa to cut the paper into small cards. Grandpa cut the cards slowly. Bennett waited. Then Bennett drew on each card. One card had a diaper. One card had a bottle. One card had a sock.

At last the baby came home. Mama laid him on the soft rug. Bennett gave him his cards, one by one. The baby grabbed the diaper card in his little hand. "That one is for you," said Bennett. "You will need it first."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Emmett sat at the dinner table. He had ten peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all.

"One, two," he said. Then he stopped. What came next? He made a mad face. He could not remember.

Big sister Mia sat next to him. She sang a little song. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door."

Emmett listened. The song was teaching him! "Three, four," he said. "Shut the door!"

He pushed one pea with his spoon. One pea went into the pile. He sang, "Five, six, pick up sticks."

Then Mom smiled. "Look at your peas, Emmett."

The peas made a round line. Red sauce was under them. It looked just like a rainbow!

Emmett sang on. "Seven, eight, lay them straight."

He laid the peas in a straight row. "Nine, ten," he sang. "A big fat hen!"

Mia laughed. Emmett ate the rainbow, one pea at a time.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
James wanted to be a rocket ship. He found a big box in the playroom. "This is my rocket," he said.

Dad came to play. "Rockets need a countdown," said Dad. "We count ten, nine, eight, all the way down to one."

"Ten, nine, eight," said James. "Seven, six, five." He patted the box. It made a boom sound. "Four, three, two, one. Blast off!" James jumped up high.

"Can I count too?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "You can do it again." James counted again, quick and loud. "Ten, nine, eight!" One jump on one. "I did it!" said James.

He sat down after his flight. He picked up his puzzle. He put in one piece, then two pieces, then three. "Rockets go up," said James. "And then they come back home." He gave his rocket box a soft pat. "Blast off tomorrow too?" asked James. Dad smiled and said, "Yes, we can count down again."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
story:
Aurora waited by the school gate. Grandma was late. Aurora's tummy felt small and tight. She held her teacher's hand.

Then Grandma came around the corner, smiling. "Sorry, sweet pea. The car was slow today." Aurora ran to her and hugged her legs.

At home, Grandma made a warm snack. Aurora ate cheese and apple slices. Then Grandma said it was bath time. Aurora took off her socks and her dress. Grandma ran the bath, and the water was warm and foamy.

Aurora rubbed the soap with water on her hands. Bubbles grew on her fingers. "Look, Grandma! Bubbles!" She patted them on her chin. Now she had a thick white soap beard. Grandma laughed and laughed. Aurora giggled too.

After the bath, Grandma helped her dry off with a big soft towel. Aurora put on her striped pajamas. She brushed her teeth with Grandma's help.

Then came a surprise. Under her pillow was a small paper star. "You put it there last night," Grandma said. Aurora smiled and held it tight. She snuggled into bed.

"Night night, Aurora," said Grandma.

"Night night, bubbles," said Aurora.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Carter went to the store with Mom. He wanted to find a squishy ball. "Stay with me," said Mom. Carter held her hand.

They walked past the bread. Then Carter saw a shelf way down the aisle. He let go of Mom's hand and skipped to the end. He looked back. He could not see Mom. He could not see her anywhere.

Carter stood very still. Then he walked back up the aisle. He passed the bread again. There was Mom! "I could not see you," said Carter. "I came back so you could see me." Mom hugged him.

They found the squishy ball. At the checkout, Carter watched Mom tap the computer screen. He held the bag. He held Mom's hand all the way to the car.

"Next time I will stay close," said Carter.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Josephine sat at the art table. She had a red crayon, a blue one, a yellow one, and a green one. She wanted to draw snow. Big soft snow, like outside her window.

She drew snow with the white crayon on white paper. She looked and looked. She could not see it. "Oh no," said Josephine. "My snow is hiding."

Then she had an idea. She took a blue paper. She drew white dots on the blue paper. They showed up! The snow was white, just like the snow outside. "Look, Ben," she said. "White snow on blue."

Ben smiled. "I want snow too," he said. Josephine did not want to be mean. So she shared her blue paper with him. He drew white snow too.

The teacher gave them a hug. "Snow pictures," she said. Josephine touched her drawing. It felt bumpy and waxy. Her white snow shone on the blue. "More snow," said Josephine, and she drew one more big white dot.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Nova put on her clean blue dress. The morning was bright and warm. Today was Eid, and there was a big festival on her street.

Mama said, "We say 'Eid Mubarak' to greet people today." Nova practiced the words in the car. "Eid Mubarak. Eid Mubarak."

At the festival, Nova smelled sweet cookies and warm bread. She heard drums. Then Auntie Salma came near the food table. Nova wanted to say hello the right way. She took a big breath. "Eid Mubarak, Auntie Salma!" Auntie Salma's face turned into a big smile. She opened her arms wide and gave Nova a hug. "Eid Mubarak to you too, little one!"

Nova tried it again on Uncle Yusuf. "Eid Mubarak!" He laughed and gave her a shiny coin. Nova gasped. The coin smelled like metal and lemons.

Every time she said the words, someone smiled back. Nova kept walking down the street. "Eid Mubarak," she called to Grandpa Omar. "Eid Mubarak!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Hayden sat at the paint table at daycare. He wanted to paint grass. The green pot was empty. Mia wanted green too. She looked grumpy.

"I need green," said Mia. "All gone."

Hayden looked at his paints. He had a red pot, a blue pot, and a yellow pot. No green. He dipped his brush in blue. He put blue on the paper. Then he dipped his brush in yellow. He put yellow right on top.

"Look!" said Hayden. The paint turned green. Green like grass. Green like the leaves outside.

Mia clapped her hands. "Green! Thank you!"

"Blue and yellow make green," said Mia. She mixed some too.

Hayden painted tall green grass. Mia painted a green frog. Then Hayden added a yellow sun. "One sun," he said. "The sun will shine on the grass."

Mia put her frog in the grass. Hayden put a blue puddle by the frog. "Splash," said Mia.

The teacher hung both paintings on the wall. "My grass," said Hayden, pointing up. "My frog," said Mia, pointing too.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Paisley stood in the restaurant kitchen. The cook, Ben, was her big friend. He let her wear a little white hat. The hat was too big, but she liked it.

"Can I help?" Paisley asked.

"Yes," said Ben. "Warm some bread first. Watch me." Ben put bread in the toaster. He got it out with a fork. Then he set warm toast on her tray.

Paisley held the butter knife. She poked a small pat of butter. She spread it on the warm toast. It was hard at first. Then it got soft. Then it got shiny. Then it went away! Paisley looked and looked. "My butter is lost!" she said.

Ben smiled. "Look at the toast," he said. The toast was wet and shiny all over. Paisley touched it with one finger. It tasted like butter. The butter was not lost. It was all over the warm toast.

"Now the milk," said Ben. Paisley lifted the little jug. She poured slowly. A drop ran down the cup. She stopped. She wiped it with a cloth. Then she poured again, very slow. No more spills.

"Paisley made breakfast," said Ben. "And you did not spill the milk."

Paisley took a big bite of toast. "It tastes like butter," she said, "all over."

Outside, a bird sat in the tree by the window. Paisley waved to it with her buttery hand.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara ran to the dress-up corner at school. Today was scarf day! She wanted to be a sleepy ocean queen with a long, wavy scarf.

She found a blue scarf. She held it up. It was so little! It went up to her elbow and stopped. "Oh no," said Clara. "This scarf is short!"

Milo came by with his scarf. His scarf went down, down, down to his shoes. "My scarf is long," said Milo.

"Long and short are opposites," said Milo.

Clara wanted a long scarf too. She looked in the box. She found a red scarf. She held it up high. Down it went, past her knees! Long!

"Look, Milo!" said Clara. She spun around fast, then slow. The scarf flapped like ocean waves. "Now I can be the ocean queen!"

"Is the ocean cold?" asked Milo.

"Pretend cold," said Clara. "Brrr!"

Milo laughed. Clara wrapped the long scarf round and round. Then she yawned a big yawn. The sleepy ocean queen lay down on the rug.

"Goodnight, ocean," said Milo.

"Goodnight," said Clara.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Violet stood by the pool. The pool was next to the big lake. Violet held her mama's hand. She wanted to swim like the big kids. But she did not want to put her face near the water.

A swim teacher named Ben knelt down. "I am your new teacher," he said. "Want to blow bubbles?" Ben put his mouth in the water. He blew out. Bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop. Violet watched the bubbles. They tickled the top of the water.

"My turn," said Violet. She held the wall. She put her mouth near the water. She blew out. Big bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! Violet laughed and laughed. Her face was wet, and it was fine. The light made the bubbles shine. "Look, Mama!" she said. She blew more bubbles. Then she kicked her feet, and Ben held her tummy. "I am swimming!" said Violet. "Again!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Amelia put her toy mouse in the box. Tommy took the toy mouse out. Amelia put it back in. Tommy pulled it out again.

"In and out are opposites," said Miss Jo. Amelia looked at the box. How odd, she thought. What goes in can come right out.

She tried it with a small red ball. In went the ball. Out came the ball. Then she tried a big teddy bear. It was too big. Only small toys fit inside.

At snack time, Amelia got cold milk. Tommy's soup was hot, so Miss Jo blew on it for him. Amelia did not touch the hot bowl. She watched Miss Jo help, from her seat.

After snack, a mouse ran across the floor. It ran so fast! Amelia tiptoed. Tiptoeing was slow. The fast mouse hid under the shelf. Could it come back out? She waited. Out it popped, quick as that.

Then it was tidy-up time. Amelia had an idea. If toys go in the box, maybe the mouse goes in its hole. She peeked at the little hole in the wall. The mouse peeked back at her.

"Hello, little mouse," she whispered. "Is that your house?"

The mouse twitched its nose. Then it popped back into its hole, tail and all.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Weston was at a big festival with his grandma. There were flags and drums and food everywhere. A long table had warm bread on it. Weston's tummy made a loud growl. "Feed me," it seemed to say.

Weston reached for the bread. Then he saw everyone sitting still. Their hands were folded, not eating. Grandma held up one finger. "We wait," she whispered. "First comes the blessing." An old man sang the blessing out loud. His voice went up and down. Weston waited, though the bread smelled so good.

Then the singing stopped. Everyone smiled and picked up bread at last. Weston took a big bite. It was warm and a little salty. "Yum," he said. "The blessing made it taste better," he whispered. Grandma laughed and gave him one more piece.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
story:
The wind blew hard outside Sienna's window. It howled and howled. Then all the lights went out. The whole apartment went dark.

"Oh no," said Sienna. "The dark!" Mommy held her hand. "The big wind knocked out the power," said Mommy. "The lights cannot work now." Daddy lit a little lantern. Mommy put a plastic cup of water on the table. Sienna's hands were wet from washing, so Mommy dried them with a towel.

They sat together on the big sofa. The lantern made a warm yellow circle. Sienna made shadows on the wall. The wind kept howling outside. Sienna was not scared. Mommy and Daddy were right there. Then the lights came back on, all at once. Sienna clapped her hands. "Hello, lights!" she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Lincoln was at Grandma's house. His new baby sister was here too. Her name was May. Grandma had made bread. Lincoln could smell it. "Can I hold the baby?" he asked. "Yes, sit on the big pillow," said Grandma. May's hand was so small. Her cheeks were soft and squishy.

At night, Lincoln slept in the little bed. He heard a cry. "Is it morning?" he asked. Grandma shook her head. "It is still night," she said. "The baby is hungry. She drinks milk many times, day and night." Mom sat in the chair and fed May. Lincoln watched from his bed. May drank and drank. Then she went back to sleep.

The next night, May cried again. "It is milk time," said Lincoln. Grandma smiled. "Yes, it is." Lincoln counted the feedings he had heard. One at bedtime. One in the dark. One when the sky turned pink. He patted May's blanket, soft and slow. "Drink your milk, baby," he whispered. "I will be here in the morning."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Nicholas had a new book. It had a bear on the front. He wanted Dad to read it, but Dad was still in the bath.

So Nicholas ran to Mom. "Can you read it?" he asked. Mom opened the book. She turned the pages from the front to the back. She read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey."

Then Dad came in, all warm and dry. "Read it too," said Nicholas. Dad sat down. He opened the book the same way. He turned the pages one by one. He read, "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey."

Nicholas blinked. Dad read the same words as Mom! "Do it again," he said. Dad read it once more. "Bear is sleepy. Bear wants honey." The words did not change. They were the same every time.

Nicholas tried it himself. He held the book upside down. The pictures looked wrong. He turned it around and started at the front. The bear was there, waiting for his honey.

"Now I know the bear's words," said Nicholas. He hugged the book tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Eloise sat on the rug in her bedroom. Her teddy bear sat on the little table by the bed. Eloise wanted to hug him. She reached out her arms.

Then she stopped. Teddy's mouth looked down, not up. His eyebrows made a frown. Eloise froze. "Teddy looks sad," she said. She picked him up and patted his back. "I will hug you." She turned his mouth up into a smile. Now Teddy looked happy. Eloise clapped. She felt so excited she jumped up and down.

The door creaked open. Eloise felt scared. She hid behind the bed. Then she heard a soft laugh. It was Mama. Mama's eyes were smiling. Her face was happy. Eloise laughed too. She ran to Mama with Teddy. "Teddy was sad. I made him smile." Mama kissed Eloise's head. "You did, sweet girl." Eloise hugged Teddy tight. Teddy smiled all night long.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Harrison went to the library with his grandma. There was a big rug on the floor. On the rug were three piles. One pile was animals. One pile was toys. One pile was foods.

Harrison picked up a black toy dog. He put it in the animal pile. Then he sat still. He looked at the toy dog. He looked at a picture of a real dog on the wall.

"Is the toy dog an animal?" he asked.
"No," said Miss Kim. "A toy dog is not alive."
"A toy dog is a toy," said Harrison.

He moved it to the toy pile. Then he sorted a red apple, a ball, and a toy cat. "A toy cat is a toy," he said. "Not alive."

Miss Kim made a happy sound. "Your sorting works now," she said.

Harrison clapped his hands. "I did it all by myself!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Anna climbed the school bus. She held her lunchbox tight. It had a plane on it. Anna loved that plane.

She sat by a boy named Sam. Sam held a lunchbox too. It had a plane on it too. "Hey, same plane!" said Sam. They laughed.

At school, the lunchboxes went on one big shelf. After lunch, Anna grabbed a box. But it was not hers. It felt too heavy. Sam opened his box and frowned. "My apple is gone," he said. "I got an apple I did not want," said Anna.

The teacher came over. "Look inside the lid," she said. Anna opened her box. There was writing on the lid. It said ANNA. Sam opened the other box. It said SAM. "That is my name!" said Anna. They swapped boxes. Anna got her own snack back. "Our names found our lunchboxes," said Anna. "Smart names," said Sam. They sat down to eat, and Anna smiled at her plane.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Myles sat on his bed. He had a fresh new book. He opened the front cover first. The pages turned one by one.

"I love this bear," said Myles. He tapped the big picture. "Who drew him?"

Myles looked at the picture. He chewed his thumb while he thought. He wanted to know. He ran to Mom.

"Who drew my bear?" he asked.

Mom opened the front of the book. She pointed to some small black marks. "Those little marks are words," she said. "Words can tell us things."

Myles leaned in close. Mom read, "It says the name of the illustrator."

"What is that?" asked Myles.

"A person who draws the pictures for a book," said Mom.

"The illustrator drew my bear!" said Myles. He ran back to his bed.

He opened the front again. He turned each page the right way. He found the bear. He found the illustrator's name too.

"The illustrator drew the dog! The illustrator drew the moon!"

Myles hugged the book. Tomorrow he would ask about a new one. "Who drew this?" he said, and pointed at the moon.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Luca stood by the bus stop with Mama. The sun came out. The sky was blue. "Sunny day," said Mama. Luca wore his yellow hat.

But then the wind blew. The wind blew his hat. Luca held his hat with both hands. "Windy now," said Mama. She zipped up his jacket.

Then the rain came. Drip, drop, drip. Mama opened a big umbrella. Luca stood under it. The rain fell and fell.

The bus came. They rode to the playground. "I want to swing," said Luca. He ran to the swings. He stopped. There was water on the ground. A big puddle sat right under the swing.

Luca looked at the sky. The rain was gone now. He looked down. The puddle was still there. "Mama! Look! Rain makes puddles on the ground," said Luca. "Yes it does," said Mama. She laughed.

Luca put on his red boots. He was ready. He gave a little spring and landed in the puddle. Splash! Water went up and up. His boots were wet. His socks were dry. "Again!" said Luca.

After splashing, they sat on the bench. Mama gave him a banana. Luca took a big bite and began to chew. "Winter will come soon," said Mama. "Then we need snow pants and mittens." "Snow!" said Luca. He pointed his banana at the sky. "Maybe tomorrow!"

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Sofia was going on a big trip. The family would sleep at a campsite. She helped put her bag in the car. "I want to sit in my seat now," she said.

Sofia climbed in fast. She held her teddy bear tight. Papa sat down and looked at her. "Where is your click?" he asked. Sofia looked around. Her car seat had straps. The straps were loose. She pushed the buckle in. Click!

"Why did we wait for that sound?" Sofia asked. "The car seat keeps you safe when we drive," said Mama. Sofia patted the buckle with her hand. Then the car started. The trees went by. Sofia pretended her teddy was buckled too. She held him up high. Click, she said softly, and smiled at the window.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Iris went to the pharmacy with Mom. Iris rubbed her hands on her pants. They felt sticky from lunch. "I want clean hands," said Iris. Mom smiled. "The pharmacist is smart about clean hands. Let's ask."

The pharmacist knelt down. She showed Iris a little bottle of soap. "We sell this soap right here," she said. "Wash for twenty seconds. Count it out." Iris wanted to try right away.

But the sink in the pharmacy bathroom was too tall. Iris stood on her toes. She could not reach the water. The pharmacist brought a step stool and stayed close by her side. Iris climbed up. The water ran over her hands! She pumped the soap. "One, two, three," she counted, all the way to twenty. The bubbles swirled down the drain. Iris held her hands up to the sun coming through the window. They were clean and shiny. "Twenty seconds!" she cheered, waving her soapy-sweet hands at Mom.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story: Henry sat in his car seat. The car went up a big hill. Then it went down a small hill. "Up and down," said Henry. The wind whooshed past the window. It was a windy day. Outside, a big truck went fast. A little blue car went slow. The sun made the seat feel hot. Henry's cup was empty. Not one drop was left. "I'm thirsty," said Henry. Dad stopped the car at a little shop. They went in to pay for some cold water. Dad held the big bottle. It was cold in his hands. The sun outside was hot. Henry found a small cup on the counter. It was empty. Dad poured the water in. The water came fast. "Stop!" said Henry. The cup was full, all the way to the top. One more drop would spill. Dad poured the next cup slow. Henry watched the water rise. He said, "Stop!" just in time. Not one drop spilled. Dad smiled. They walked back to the car. Henry held his full cup with two hands. He drank it all down. Now the cup was empty again. The car drove on, slow and steady, over the next big hill.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story: Daniel went to the park with Grandma. He wanted to splash in the big puddle by the bench. He took off one shoe. He put in his toe. Splash! The water was cold. Then Daniel saw something shiny in the grass. It was a little lighter. It did not belong to anyone at the park. Daniel did not pick it up. He kept his hands behind his back. He walked to Grandma. "I found a little lighter," he said. Grandma looked at it. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," she said. She picked it up and put it in her pocket. "Good job telling me." Daniel went back to the puddle. He put in his whole foot. Splash! Splash! The sun went down. It was getting late. "One more splash," said Grandma, "then we go home."
